t.2.9.1: Thus addressed, Kaikeyī, her face blazing with anger, heaved a long, hot sigh and spoke these words to Mantharā.
t.2.9.2: Today I shall swiftly send Rāma away to the forest, and I shall have Bharata quickly consecrated as heir apparent.
t.2.9.3: But now, Mantharā, consider this: by what means might Bharata obtain the kingdom, and Rāma by no means at all?
t.2.9.4: Thus addressed by that queen, the evil-minded Mantharā, seeking to harm Rāma's cause, spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
t.2.9.5: Come now, I shall tell you, Kaikeyī, and let it be heard from me, how your son Bharata will obtain the kingdom all to himself.
t.2.9.6: Having heard these words of Mantharā, Kaikayī rose a little from her well-spread couch and spoke thus.
t.2.9.7: Tell me the means, O Mantharā: by what means may Bharata obtain the kingdom, and Rāma by no means at all?
t.2.9.9: In the war between the gods and the asuras, your husband, together with the royal sages, went forth taking you with him, to render aid to the king of the gods.
t.2.9.8: Thus addressed by the queen, the evil-minded hunchback Mantharā, intent on harming Rāma's interests, spoke these words.
t.2.9.10: O Kaikeyī, in the southern direction, toward the Daṇḍaka forests, there is a city renowned as Vaijayanta, where Timidhvaja dwelt.
t.2.9.11: That great asura, renowned as Śambara and master of a hundred magical arts, unconquered by the hosts of the gods, gave battle to Śakra.
t.2.9.12: Then, in that great battle, O queen, King Daśaratha, who had lost consciousness, was carried away by you from the field of combat.
t.2.9.13: There too, when your husband was wounded by weapons, he was protected by you; and he, pleased, granted you two boons, O lovely one.
t.2.9.14: You said to your husband, O queen, 'When I wish, then I shall claim the two boons,' and that great-souled one replied, 'So be it.' For I knew nothing of this myself, O queen; it was you yourself who told it to me long ago.
t.2.9.15: Ask your husband for those two boons: the consecration of Bharata, and the banishment of Rāma for fourteen years.
t.2.9.16: Daughter of Aśvapati, enter the chamber of anger today as if enraged, and lie down on the bare ground in soiled garments. Do not look up at him, and do not speak to him.
t.2.9.17: You are ever beloved of your husband; of this I have no doubt. For your sake the great king would even enter fire.
t.2.9.18: He is not able to anger you, nor to look upon you when you are angry; for the king would give up even his life for the sake of what is dear to you.
t.2.9.19: For the lord of the earth cannot transgress your word. O you of dull nature, recognize the power of your own good fortune as the beloved wife!
t.2.9.20: King Daśaratha may offer you gems, pearls, gold and jewels of many kinds, but do not set your mind on them.
t.2.9.21: Those two boons which Daśaratha granted you in the war between the gods and the asuras, remind him of them, O fortunate lady; let not that purpose pass you by.
t.2.9.22: But when Rāghava himself, having raised you up, would offer you a boon, then, having first made the great king firm in his promise, you should choose this boon.
t.2.9.23: Banish Rāma to the forest for nine years and five. Let Bharata, a bull among kings, be made king over the earth.
t.2.9.25: By the time Rāma returns from the forest, your son will have become firmly rooted, self-possessed, and will have won the people over to his side together with his friends.
t.2.9.24: Once he is banished in this way, Rāma will no longer be the delight of anyone, and Bharata, his enemies slain, will become your king.
t.2.9.26: I think the time has come for you: free from fear, restrain the king and make him turn back from his resolve to consecrate Rāma.
t.2.9.27: Then, made by her to take what was harmful in the guise of what was good, Kaikeyī, delighted and confident, said this to Mantharā.
t.2.9.28: O hunchback, I have not truly known you as the excellent one, the one who gives the best counsel. Of all the hunchbacks on earth, you are the foremost in firmness of judgment.
t.2.9.29: It is you alone, O Kubjā, ever devoted to my interests and wishing my good; I myself would not have perceived what the king intends to do.
t.2.9.30: There are hunchbacks who are misshapen, crooked and exceedingly wicked, but you are bent like a lotus bowed by the wind, and lovely to behold.
t.2.9.31: Your breast is firmly set and rises high, up to your shoulders, and below it your belly lies flat and still, with a lovely navel, as though it were abashed.
t.2.9.33: O Mantharā, clad in fine linen, as you walk ahead of me on your long thighs, you shine like a royal swan.
t.2.9.32: Your hips, adorned with a girdle-string, ring with its jingling; your shanks are set very close together, and both your feet are long.
t.2.9.34: This hump of yours, long and broad like the projecting front of a chariot, is where your counsels, your knowledge of statecraft, and your wiles reside.
t.2.9.35: O hunchbacked one, when Bharata has been consecrated and Rāghava has gone to the forest, I shall then fasten upon you a garland of gold.
t.2.9.36: And, O lovely one, once I have gained my object and am content, I shall have your hump overlaid with pure, well-refined gold.
t.2.9.37: And on your face, O hunchbacked one, I shall have a bright, beautiful tilaka made of gold, and lovely ornaments as well, made for you.
t.2.9.39: Hunchbacks adorned with every ornament shall wait upon your feet too, O hunchback, just as you always wait upon mine.
t.2.9.38: Dressed in a fine garment, you will move about like a goddess; peerless of countenance, with a face that challenges the moon, you will attain the foremost station, lording it over your enemies.
t.2.9.40: Being praised thus, she said this to Kaikeyī, who was lying on her bright bed like a tongue of flame upon an altar.
t.2.9.42: Thus urged on, the large-eyed queen, proud and intoxicated with her good fortune as the favoured wife, went together with Mantharā to the chamber of anger.
t.2.9.41: When the water has already flowed away, no dam is built, O fair lady. Rise, do what is to your good, and show yourself to the king.
t.2.9.43: The beautiful woman took off her pearl necklace worth many hundreds of thousands, along with her other lovely ornaments, fit for the noblest.
t.2.9.45: Either, O Kubjā, you will report to the king that I have died here, or else, when Rāghava has gone to the forest, Bharata will obtain the earth.
t.2.9.44: Then Kaikeyī, radiant like gold, having fallen under the sway of the hunchback's words, lay down there on the ground and said this to Mantharā.
t.2.9.46: Then, having spoken these exceedingly cruel words, the passionate lady laid aside all her ornaments and lay down upon the bare ground, uncovered by any spread, like a fallen kiṃnarī.
t.2.9.47: Her face veiled in the darkness of her surging wrath, and having likewise cast off her finest garlands and ornaments, that wife of the lord of men grew sullen at heart, like the sky shrouded in darkness, its stars sunk from sight.
